<meta>continues from previous page: drinking from the boundless.</meta> Laozi remained indifferent and did not respond.

The next day, Shi Chengqi saw him again and said:
"Yesterday, I had a sharp criticism for you. Today, my mind has truly withdrawn <margin>"Withdrawal" is like "regret."</margin> from it. Why is this?"

Laozi said: "As for the clever, the wise, the divine, and the sagely, I thought I had cast off such labels. <margin>Word usage note.</margin> Yesterday, if you had called me an ox, I would have called myself an ox. If you had called me a horse, I would have called myself a horse. <margin>Insufficient.</margin> If the reality is present and someone gives it a name, <margin>Word usage note.</margin> yet one refuses to accept it, one receives a double calamity. <margin>To struggle against the name again would bring disaster upon oneself.</margin> My compliance <margin>It is always like this.</margin> is constant; I do not comply for the sake of 'wearing' a performance of compliance." <margin>"Compliance" <note>original: 服</note> here does not mean a garment to be put on and worn; it is like the "compliance" of holding something close to the heart.</margin> <margin>Sentence structure note.</margin>

Shi Chengqi walked with his chest forward <margin>What I practice.</margin> <note>showing deep respect</note>, avoiding his own shadow <margin>The appearance of turning the body aside <note>to show deference</note>.</margin>, stepping carefully <margin>This is proof that restraint has reached its limit.</margin>

<summary>In this passage, the seeker Shi Chengqi returns to Laozi with a changed heart, leading Laozi to explain how he remains indifferent to external labels like horse or ox. Laozi emphasizes that resisting names when the underlying reality exists only brings misfortune, advocating for a natural, inward compliance.</summary>
<keywords>Laozi, Shi Chengqi, names and reality, indifference, compliance, Daoism, ox and horse metaphor</keywords>
